whyCorrect: Read to the end of the passage before you punctuate. After the blank there is a complete sentence waiting to happen: these elected officials take turns serving as the office's chairperson has its own subject and verb. So whatever fills the blank has to close the first sentence off, and only a period does that. With D you get one full sentence, Bosnia and Herzegovina does not have one president but three, and then a second sentence that opens with the modifier Known as members of the office of the presidency, adds the appositive list, and lands on the subject these elected officials.

whyWrong.A: Attaching who are known keeps everything in one sentence, so these elected officials take turns serving is a second independent clause hooked on with only a comma.
whyWrong.B: The comma plus participle keeps the first clause running, leaving these elected officials take turns serving spliced onto it.
whyWrong.C: Same problem as A with extra punctuation: the relative clause does not end the sentence, so the final independent clause is still spliced on.

commonMistakes: Choosing among the three comma versions without noticing that the words after the list already form a complete sentence.
tips: When a long modifier sits between the blank and the end, check whether the words after it can stand alone; if they can, the blank usually needs a period.

whyCorrect: Test each side of the blank on its own. The guide soon grew in scope and influence is a complete sentence, and its modest French eateries were replaced with some of the most esteemed restaurants from around the world is a complete sentence too. Two independent clauses join with a comma plus a coordinating conjunction, which is exactly what C supplies.

whyWrong.A: A comma alone between two independent clauses is a comma splice.
whyWrong.B: The conjunction without the comma leaves the two independent clauses fused; and needs the comma when it joins full clauses.
whyWrong.D: No punctuation at all runs the two independent clauses straight together.

commonMistakes: Seeing the earlier scope and influence pairing and assuming the second and is also joining two nouns.
tips: Cover everything after the blank and ask whether it could be its own sentence; that decides comma-versus-comma-plus-and.

whyCorrect: The sentence already has its main verb: The chapter ... was the subject of a profile. The blank therefore cannot hold another conjugated verb, because there is no conjunction to join a second clause. What it needs is a modifier describing the profile, and the participle appearing does that job: a profile appearing in the Navajo Times.

whyWrong.A: appeared is a finite past-tense verb, giving the sentence a second main verb with nothing joining it to the first.
whyWrong.C: appears is finite as well, and its present tense also clashes with the past-tense was.
whyWrong.D: Besides being misspelled, has appeared is another finite verb the sentence has no room for.

tips: When the sentence already has a subject and a main verb, the blank almost always wants an -ing or -ed modifier, not another conjugated verb.

whyCorrect: The sentence before the blank says the 424 BCE eclipse was annular; the sentence after it explains what annular means, that the Moon left a visible ring rather than covering the Sun. That is a restatement in plainer terms, not a new fact, so the transition has to signal in other words.

whyWrong.A: Meanwhile marks two things happening at the same time, but the second sentence is not a separate simultaneous event; it defines the first.
whyWrong.C: For example would need the second sentence to be one instance of a general category, but it describes the same eclipse the previous sentence just named.
whyWrong.D: Nonetheless signals a contrast, and nothing in the definition of annular pushes back against the claim that the eclipse was annular.

commonMistakes: Treating any explanatory follow-up as an example; a definition of a term you just used is a restatement, not an example.

whyCorrect: Line up the two facts: the JWST is primarily an infrared telescope, and most light from distant galaxies is infrared. The clause after the blank draws the payoff from those facts, that the JWST tells van Campen's team far more about distant galaxies than Hubble could. The transition has to reinforce and extend the point, not turn against it, which leaves in fact.

whyWrong.A: besides introduces a separate additional argument, but this clause is the conclusion that follows from the infrared point, not a new point alongside it.
whyWrong.B: however signals contrast, and the JWST's advantage agrees with what came before rather than opposing it.
whyWrong.C: on the contrary is even stronger, used to reject a preceding statement, and nothing here is being rejected.

tips: Decide first whether the relationship is agreement or contrast; that eliminates half the choices before you weigh the fine shades.

whyCorrect: The first sentence promises a range of outcomes, and the sentence before the blank gives one outcome: many islands became independent nations. The sentence after the blank gives the opposite outcome, islands that remained part of the US or of French Polynesia. That flip is what the transition must mark.

whyWrong.A: For example would make the Northern Marianas and the Society Islands instances of islands that became independent, and they are the opposite.
whyWrong.B: Therefore claims the second sentence follows as a consequence of widespread independence, which it does not.
whyWrong.C: In fact would intensify the independence claim, but the sentence undercuts it instead.

commonMistakes: Reading the pair as example-and-illustration because both sentences list islands, without checking that the second list contradicts the first.

whyCorrect: The goal has two parts: describe Silver Upper White River, and do it for an audience meeting the work for the first time. That means the sentence has to supply the work's own details, its date, its recycled-silver material, and its gallery-wall scale, without leaning on anything the reader is assumed to know already. A delivers exactly those notes and nothing else.

whyWrong.B: It names the work but describes Maya Lin's reputation instead of the artwork, so a new audience learns nothing about what the piece is.
whyWrong.C: It spends most of its length on Women's Table and reduces Silver Upper White River to the bare label an installation artwork.
whyWrong.D: It describes the work only by comparison to Women's Table, which a new audience has no reason to be familiar with.

tips: When the goal names a target audience, drop any choice that assumes the audience already knows a second subject.

whyCorrect: To contrast two things you have to state a property of each and let them differ. A does that on one axis, chemical composition: dichloromethane is hydrogen, chlorine and carbon, while tetradecafluorohexane is fluorine and carbon. The semicolon sets the two descriptions against each other, which is the contrast the goal asks for.

whyWrong.B: It groups the two compounds under a shared label, which states a similarity rather than a difference.
whyWrong.C: The word both gives the game away: it lists what the compounds have in common instead of contrasting them.
whyWrong.D: It discusses only tetradecafluorohexane, so there is nothing for it to be contrasted with.

commonMistakes: Accepting a sentence that mentions both compounds as a contrast; mentioning both is necessary but not sufficient, they must be set against each other.

whyCorrect: The goal is narrow: specify the climate of the test site. Only two notes describe climate, that the site was a mesic grassland in Argentina and that it sat in a subtropical climate with year-round rain. A is the one choice that carries those climate details into the sentence; everything else in the notes is about the study's design or result.

whyWrong.B: It says the study looked at a given climate without ever saying which one, so it names the goal instead of meeting it.
whyWrong.C: It specifies what plant litter is and where the study happened, but says nothing about climate.
whyWrong.D: It reports the study's finding, which is a different goal entirely.

tips: When the goal names one specific detail, scan the notes for the lines that carry that detail and keep only the choice built from them.

whyCorrect: The sentence sets Mocsáry against the Van Burens, and the clause about the Van Burens ends with a deed for which they will always be remembered. Their place in historical memory is settled and secure, so the comparison needs a word saying that Mocsáry's place is the opposite of secure. Uncertain is the only choice that supplies that contrast; the but after accomplished much is the signal that the sentence is heading toward a shortfall.

whyWrong.A: Enduring makes her memory more lasting than that of women who will always be remembered, which reverses the contrast the sentence sets up.
whyWrong.B: Conspicuous means noticeable, again crediting her with a more prominent memory rather than a shakier one.
whyWrong.C: Deserving shifts to whether the memory is merited, but the passage already grants that she accomplished much; what is in question is whether she is remembered.

commonMistakes: Reading undoubtedly accomplished much as the sentence's point and picking a positive word, when the but turns the sentence the other way.

whyCorrect: The first sentence states the conclusion outright: the reception has been very good. The blank has to name reviewer behavior consistent with that, and the award mentioned right after confirms it. Praised is the only choice that matches a good reception.

whyWrong.A: Overlooked means the reviewers ignored the book, which cannot follow from many reviewers have in a sentence about a very good reception.
whyWrong.B: Misunderstood describes a failure of reading, not the positive response the passage reports.
whyWrong.D: Attacked is the direct opposite of a good reception.

tips: When a sentence states the overall verdict up front, the blank almost always just restates that verdict in specific terms.

whyCorrect: The colon means the second half defines the first. What follows is cuttlefish routinely showing restraint and delaying gratification, which is a description of doing something well. The blank sits in surprisingly ___ at exercising self-control, so it needs an adjective for skill or ability, and competent is the only one.

whyWrong.A: Awkward would mean they are bad at self-control, contradicting the evidence after the colon.
whyWrong.B: Imaginative describes creativity, which is not what waiting for a preferred treat demonstrates.
whyWrong.C: Manageable describes something that can be handled by someone else, so it makes the cuttlefish the object of control rather than the ones exercising it.

commonMistakes: Grabbing a generally positive word without checking that it fits the frame ___ at doing something, which requires a word about ability.

whyCorrect: The sentence lists a range of art across the city and says Chicago offers these works to do something to the tastes of art lovers. The logical relationship is that the variety is enough to satisfy those tastes, and satiate means to satisfy fully.

whyWrong.A: Mitigate means to lessen something bad, but a taste for art is not a harm to be reduced.
whyWrong.C: Venerate means to revere, and the art works do not worship the tastes of art lovers.
whyWrong.D: Supplant means to replace, which would mean the art drives out the very tastes it appeals to.

tips: Plug each word into the frame works to ___ the tastes of art lovers and read it aloud; three of the four produce something no one would say.

whyCorrect: Sort out which way the causation runs. The fact stated at the end, that flight features limit top speed less than running features do, is the cause; the speed gap between the pronghorn and the frigatebird is the result. The blank names what the difference is relative to that fact, so it has to be the effect: the difference is largely a consequence of it.

whyWrong.B: An objective would make the speed difference a goal something is aiming at, but nothing here has intentions.
whyWrong.C: A repudiation would mean the difference rejects the fact, when the fact is what accounts for the difference.
whyWrong.D: An explanation reverses the causation: the fact explains the difference, not the other way around.

commonMistakes: Picking an explanation because the sentence is clearly explaining something, without checking which item is doing the explaining.

whyCorrect: Walk the text in order. It opens by describing what Villasana makes and how, then gives two named examples, the Prince portrait and the girl on the sidewalk, and closes by saying Villasana sees both approaches as ways of depicting the power and interconnectedness of all people. That final sentence is an artistic goal, so the structure is description, examples, and then the purpose behind them.

whyWrong.A: The text never discusses her cultural background as a formative influence, and it mentions no future projects.
whyWrong.B: No other contemporary artists appear, and the two works are set against each other with However rather than shown to be similar.
whyWrong.C: There is no history of yarn in art and no claim about how popular her work is.

tips: For structure questions, check every clause of the choice; one wrong stage is enough to eliminate it.

whyCorrect: The text's shape is a concession followed by a claim: writing a sonnet sequence is intrinsically challenging, yet poets from Brooks to Nelson keep writing them, likely because the form lets a poet display virtuosity and ingenuity. That last clause is the point the whole passage builds to, so the purpose is to offer a reason the genre still attracts poets despite its difficulty.

whyWrong.A: Brooks and Nelson are named only as poets who took the form up; no innovation of theirs is described.
whyWrong.B: The text draws no comparison in quality or creativity between the earlier and later poets, only that both wrote sonnet sequences.
whyWrong.C: The difficulty is asserted in a single subordinate clause and never broken down into structural features.

commonMistakes: Choosing the option built from the concession, the difficulty of the form, rather than from the claim the concession is setting up.

whyCorrect: Text 2 does not deny that the fleeing-audience story is told; it denies that any contemporary evidence supports it, and then explains why it survives anyway. Its explanation is that our conviction about how transformative film was is so strong that we manufactured a founding myth to match. Applied to Text 1, which retells the story and calls it a major cultural shift, that means the description is driven by a sense of film's significance rather than by the record.

whyWrong.A: The first half is right, but Text 2 says the myth splits audiences into a naïve past and a sophisticated present; it never says historians think themselves superior to today's audiences.
whyWrong.B: Text 2 says the story is canonical even among film historians, so historians share the belief rather than dismissing it as naïve.
whyWrong.D: Text 2's whole point is that there is no contemporary evidence of alarm, so the story cannot be capturing what early audiences actually felt.

tips: For cross-text questions, find the sentence in Text 2 that explains why the other view exists; that sentence is usually the answer in paraphrase.

whyCorrect: The last sentence contrasts the two methods directly: conventional methods move energy from the surface inward, while infrared generates heat inside the food, thus reducing industrial cooking times. If infrared reduces cooking times, the conventional methods it improves on must have longer ones. That is the only drawback the text actually states.

whyWrong.A: Technological breakdowns are never mentioned.
whyWrong.B: The text says nothing about the size or weight of foods either method can handle; it does mention large batches, but as something the industry has long done.
whyWrong.D: Energy is discussed only as something transferred or generated, never as an amount consumed by one method versus another.

commonMistakes: Assuming a slower method must also be a more energy-hungry one; the text supports only the timing claim.

whyCorrect: Use the two numbers the text gives. A sei whale reaches at most 25,000 kg and a baleen whale eats up to 30 percent of its mass per day, which caps the sei whale near 7,500 kg of krill. The bowhead is stated to consume as much as 19,800 kg per day. So the bowhead's daily krill intake is the larger of the two.

whyWrong.A: Competition for food is never raised; the text only compares sizes and intake.
whyWrong.B: 19,800 kg is roughly 79 percent of the sei whale's maximum mass, far above the 30 percent daily figure the text gives.
whyWrong.C: The text says the sei whale, like all baleen whales, feeds on krill, so there is no difference in likelihood.

tips: When a passage gives a percentage and a mass, do the multiplication before comparing; the comparison is usually the whole question.

whyCorrect: Walsh's finding has two linked parts: users become more aware of how their listening might look to others, and that awareness then changes what they actually do. The quotation you want has to show both. B does, with a user choosing songs for the friends who follow them instead of what they would otherwise want to hear at that moment.

whyWrong.A: It contrasts streaming with buying records; it is about passivity, not about awareness of an audience.
whyWrong.C: It concerns the platform's recommendation algorithm, which has nothing to do with the social dimensions Walsh studied.
whyWrong.D: It reports a pleasant social side effect but shows no change in what the user chooses to listen to, so it misses the second half of the finding.

commonMistakes: Settling for a quotation that merely mentions friends; the finding requires the awareness of others to alter the listening behavior.

whyCorrect: The conclusion is that telling real laughter from forced laughter works the same way everywhere. It is strengthened by anything showing the cue listeners rely on is itself culture-independent. D supplies exactly that: a reliable acoustic difference in pitch that holds regardless of the speakers' society, so listeners anywhere have the same signal to work from.

whyWrong.A: Variation in spontaneous laughter both within and across societies makes the cue less consistent, which pulls against universality rather than supporting it.
whyWrong.B: Tying listeners' judgments to a feature of their society, community size, points to cultural variation in the ability, the opposite of the conclusion.
whyWrong.C: Judging how well two people know each other is a different skill, and it is reported for only two of the 21 societies.

tips: To strengthen a universality claim, look for evidence that the underlying mechanism does not change from group to group.

whyCorrect: The critic's alternative explanation is that the lullaby captured the infants' attention rather than relaxing them. The last sentence hands you the test: pupils get larger when attention is captured. So if pupils were smaller during the lullaby than during the non-lullaby, attention was not heightened during the lullaby and the critic's explanation for the slower heart rate collapses.

whyWrong.A: Equal blinking says attention did not differ, but it does not use the measure the passage sets up and leaves the critic room to argue about how blinking relates to attention; the pupil evidence contradicts the claim outright.
whyWrong.B: Unfamiliarity with the language and melody says nothing about whether the infants were relaxed or merely attentive.
whyWrong.D: What parents believe about the songs is an opinion, not evidence about the infants' physiological response.

commonMistakes: Forgetting that larger pupils mean more attention, and so reading the smaller-pupil finding as support for the critic.

whyCorrect: Follow the chain. The borrowed words entered Mayan languages while the Olmecs dominated the region, and every one of them comes from the Zoque branch specifically, not from Mixe-Zoquean generally. For a word to be identifiably Zoque rather than simply Mixe-Zoquean, the Zoque branch has to have existed as a distinct branch at the time of borrowing. So the split into Mixe and Zoque must already have happened by the Olmec period.

whyWrong.A: If Mixe languages had replaced Zoque ones before 1500 BCE, the borrowed words could not all be Zoque in origin.
whyWrong.C: The text traces words moving from Mixe-Zoquean into Mayan only; nothing is said about donations to other Mixe-Zoquean languages.
whyWrong.D: The text explicitly calls the Mayan languages otherwise unrelated to the Mixe-Zoquean family, so no Mixe-Zoquean language founded it.

tips: When a passage stresses a word like all or tellingly, the inference usually turns on what that specificity requires to have been true earlier.

whyCorrect: The blank follows if this view is correct, so it has to state the shortcoming the ecosystem view attributes to the single-species approach. That view's defining claim is that species interact with the climate, terrain, and other species around them. Concentrating on M. anniana alone therefore leaves out the effects of the other Tamaulipas species it depends on or competes with.

whyWrong.B: The single-species approach keeps the focus squarely on M. anniana; that is what it is, not a failure of it.
whyWrong.C: A better understanding of distribution would be a benefit, but the sentence is setting up a drawback, and distribution across Mexico is not what the ecosystem view adds.
whyWrong.D: The single-species approach is precisely the one that does not take the surrounding climate and competing species into account.

commonMistakes: Writing a criticism of the ecosystem approach instead of the single-species one; check which approach the sentence's subject names.

whyCorrect: The name identifies which essayist the editors turned to, so it is essential to the noun phrase and takes no punctuation at all: turned to the essayist Carolyn Servid to craft the entry. Nothing interrupts the sentence between the verb and its object, and nothing interrupts the object and the infinitive that follows.

whyWrong.A: A single comma before the name separates the essayist from the name that identifies it and leaves the following comma unpaired.
whyWrong.B: Paired commas mark the name as extra information the sentence could drop, but the editors turned to the essayist to craft the entry leaves the reader with no idea who was asked.
whyWrong.C: The comma after the name cuts the object away from the infinitive to craft, which belongs to it.

tips: Ask whether removing the name still tells the reader who is meant; if it does not, use no commas.

whyCorrect: Find the subject of the blank by tracing the relative pronoun. That refers back to items, which is plural, so the verb has to be plural. The passage is set in an empire that ended in 1453, and the surrounding verbs are past tense, so the plural past were is what fits.

whyWrong.A: has been is singular and its present-perfect tense claims the demand continues today.
whyWrong.C: was is singular, but the subject items is plural.
whyWrong.D: is is both singular and present tense, putting a long-vanished empire's trade goods in demand now.

commonMistakes: Letting the nearest noun, iron or demand, set the verb number instead of the actual subject items.

whyCorrect: The blank is the object of taught, and what Aristotle taught is the ideas named earlier in the sentence. Ideas is plural, so the pronoun standing in for it must be plural too. Only them is.

whyWrong.A: it is singular and has no singular noun in the sentence to refer to.
whyWrong.B: that is singular and, used alone as a pronoun, points to a single thing or a whole situation rather than to a set of ideas.
whyWrong.C: this is singular for the same reason and also suggests something just introduced rather than the plural ideas already named.

tips: Pronoun questions come down to finding the noun the pronoun replaces and matching its number.

whyCorrect: This is a list of three deserts, and each item already contains a comma of its own: the Syrian Desert, ranked ninth in size; the Kyzylkum Desert, ranked sixteenth; and the Chalbi Desert, ranked twenty-ninth. When list items contain internal commas, the items are separated by semicolons, which is what B supplies at both junctions.

whyWrong.A: It puts a comma where the list items divide and a semicolon inside the second item, exactly reversing the two marks.
whyWrong.C: With no punctuation after ninth in size, the first and second list items run together.
whyWrong.D: The semicolon after Kyzylkum Desert cuts that item off from its own modifier ranked sixteenth, which describes it.

tips: Semicolons separate list items only when the items themselves contain commas; check where the internal commas fall before placing them.

whyCorrect: Look for the verb the relative clause already has. In whose work ___ the richness of Yearsley's poems and the poet's historical importance ... encourages a broader rethinking, the main verb is encourages and its subject is work. The blank therefore cannot be a second conjugated verb; it has to be a participle modifying work, so highlighting is the only option that leaves the clause with exactly one main verb.

whyWrong.A: highlights is finite, giving work two main verbs with no conjunction between them.
whyWrong.C: has highlighted is finite as well, and the same double-verb problem results.
whyWrong.D: is highlighting is finite too; the length of the sentence hides the clash but does not remove it.

commonMistakes: Reading only as far as the blank, where a conjugated verb sounds right, and never reaching encourages.

whyCorrect: A semicolon has to have an independent clause on each side, so the blank must supply a real verb for its vehicles. That rules out the bare participle. Between the tenses, the surrounding sentence uses the present, this period ... is remembered, and collectors prize these cars now, so the present passive are highly prized keeps the two halves consistent.

whyWrong.A: highly prized is a participle with no helping verb, leaving a fragment after the semicolon.
whyWrong.B: had been highly prized is past perfect, which places the collecting before some earlier past event the sentence never names.
whyWrong.D: were highly prized is grammatical but shifts to the past, contradicting the present-tense is remembered and implying collectors no longer value the cars.

tips: After a semicolon, first check that a subject and a real verb are present, then check the tense against the clause before it.

whyCorrect: The first sentence describes an ongoing push, with countries still seeking advantage in space as technology advances, and the second names the one thing that holds that push in check: a 1967 treaty signed by more than 100 nations that keeps space neutral. The treaty is being presented as the final, overriding constraint on all that ambition, which is what Ultimately marks.

whyWrong.A: Consequently makes the treaty a result of the ambitions, but the passage describes those ambitions as continuing now while the treaty dates from 1967, so the causation would run backward in time.
whyWrong.B: Specifically would make the treaty a narrower instance of nations seeking advantage, and the treaty restrains that behavior instead of illustrating it.
whyWrong.C: Alternatively offers a competing option of the same kind, and a binding multinational treaty is not another way for a country to pursue advantage in space.

commonMistakes: Seeing that the treaty opposes the ambitions and reaching for a cause-and-effect word; the treaty is the standing limit on them, not their product.

whyCorrect: Compare what the two sentences actually claim. The first says the researchers determined the ratio of three plant subtypes in elk diets; the second says they determined the relative quantities of the plants the animals ate. Those are the same act described in plainer words, so the transition has to signal a restatement.

whyWrong.B: In addition would make the second sentence a further, separate finding, but it reports no new measurement.
whyWrong.C: By contrast requires the second sentence to differ from the first, and it says the same thing.
whyWrong.D: Next would make it a later step in a procedure, but determining a ratio and determining relative quantities are one step, not two.

tips: If the second sentence uses everyday words for the technical term in the first, you are looking at a restatement.

whyCorrect: The middle sentence supplies the rule: the Roman numeral records naming order, not distance from the planet. The last sentence draws the conclusion that follows from that rule, namely that you cannot read Jupiter VII as the seventh-closest moon. A conclusion drawn from what was just said calls for then.

whyWrong.A: however signals a reversal, but the final sentence agrees with the rule stated before it and applies it.
whyWrong.C: moreover would add a second, separate point, while this sentence is the payoff of the point already made.
whyWrong.D: finally marks the last item in a list or sequence, and no sequence has been running.

tips: When the last sentence tells you what you may not conclude, check whether it follows from the previous sentence; if it does, you need an inference word, not a contrast word.

whyCorrect: The goal is to emphasize a difference, so the sentence has to name both birds and set one feature of each against the other. B does that on the bill shape: the great-billed hermit's is curved, the amethyst woodstar's is straight. The contrast word whereas is what makes the difference the point of the sentence rather than a detail in it.

whyWrong.A: It describes only the great-billed hermit, so there is nothing for its features to differ from.
whyWrong.C: It names both birds but groups them together as members of the same set, which is a similarity.
whyWrong.D: It describes only the amethyst woodstar.

commonMistakes: Picking a choice that mentions both birds without actually opposing a feature of one to a feature of the other.

whyCorrect: The goal names two specific minerals, talc and quartz, so the correct sentence has to compare those two and no others. Quartz is a 7 and talc is a 1, and the notes say a higher-numbered mineral is harder and can leave visible scratches on a lower-numbered one. D states that relationship for exactly the pair the goal asks about.

whyWrong.A: It lists three minerals and describes what the scale does, without saying which of talc and quartz is harder.
whyWrong.B: It compares fluorite and talc, so quartz never enters the comparison.
whyWrong.C: It compares quartz and fluorite, leaving talc out.

tips: When the goal names two specific items, eliminate every choice that swaps one of them for a third.

whyCorrect: The goal asks for a detailed overview of the structures, so the sentence should carry as many of the architectural notes as possible: the cliff alcove setting, the multistory adobe and stone buildings, the cube-shaped contiguous rooms, and the round kivas they surround. C packs all four in; the other choices each keep one detail and drop the rest.

whyWrong.A: It describes kivas only, so it covers one room type rather than the settlement's structures as a whole.
whyWrong.B: It gives who built Keet Seel, where, and when, which is history rather than a description of the buildings.
whyWrong.D: It names only the building materials, which is a single detail, not an overview.

tips: For an overview or detailed description goal, count how many relevant notes each choice actually uses.

whyCorrect: The not only ... but also frame pairs the blank with illuminate, so the blank needs a verb of the same kind, something the fossil lets researchers come to understand. Discern means to make out or perceive clearly, which is what you do with steps in an evolutionary sequence.

whyWrong.A: Exploit means to use for advantage, which does not apply to steps in hominid evolution.
whyWrong.B: Prioritize means to rank by importance, but the fossil helps researchers detect the steps, not rank them.
whyWrong.C: Yield means to produce or give up; the fossil might yield information, but paleoanthropologists do not yield evolutionary steps.

tips: In a not only ... but also sentence, the second verb tells you what kind of verb the blank has to be.

whyCorrect: The sentence turns on inaccessible until, so the blank names the state the data reached once the transfer project finished, which is the opposite of inaccessible. The next sentence confirms it: Weber can now use the information. Available is the direct opposite of inaccessible.

whyWrong.A: Complicated describes difficulty of a different kind and would not explain how Weber came to use the data.
whyWrong.B: Representative concerns how well a sample stands for a whole, which the passage never raises.
whyWrong.D: Predictable describes the content of the data, not whether anyone can reach it.

tips: When a sentence contains until, the blank usually names the reversal of the state described just before it.

whyCorrect: The first sentence says humanoid features exist so that people find robots easier to interact with, and the blank sits in the concessive half of a while sentence that grants that benefit before naming the uncanny-valley risk. So the blank must be a verb for producing that comfort in people. Engender means to bring about or give rise to.

whyWrong.B: Constrict means to narrow or squeeze, which would have the features reducing comfort, contradicting the stated purpose.
whyWrong.C: Counterbalance means to offset, again working against the comfort rather than creating it.
whyWrong.D: Repudiate means to reject a claim, which cannot be done to a feeling.

commonMistakes: Letting the uncanny-valley warning at the end pull you toward a negative verb; the while clause is where the positive effect is conceded.

whyCorrect: The temptation named in the first half is treating one case, Detroit's car firms, as representative of industrial agglomeration in general, and the colon explains why that fails: the labor pools driving collocation there were largely absent from toy manufacturing. So what Faggio and colleagues caution against is generalizing outward from a single case, which is what extrapolating from means.

whyWrong.A: Convening with means meeting together, which cannot be done with an example.
whyWrong.C: Corroborating means confirming with further evidence, and there is no claim here that the example is being used to confirm.
whyWrong.D: Scrutinizing means examining closely, but close examination of Detroit is not the error; drawing a general rule from it is.

tips: The word after the blank tells you what the verb acts on; this one example points to a verb about generalizing, not about studying.

whyCorrect: The sentence opens by saying certain features appear in almost every mosque design, and the ablution area is offered as one of them. The second sentence reinforces the point: even stylistically mixed mosques include these standard features. So the blank needs a word for a defining, characteristic feature, which is what a hallmark is.

whyWrong.A: A duplicate is a copy of something else, but the ablution area is not a copy of mosque architecture.
whyWrong.B: A motivation is a reason for acting, and a washing area is a physical feature rather than a reason anyone builds.
whyWrong.C: A rejection reverses the sentence, since the feature is nearly universal rather than refused.

tips: Words like almost always included and standard signal that the blank means characteristic or defining.

whyCorrect: Track the text sentence by sentence. It starts with two specific Ojibwe words and their meanings, then names and defines the general phenomenon those words illustrate, reduplication, shows how it applies to those exact words, and closes by saying the phenomenon is common in Ojibwe. C is that sequence: examples first, the general principle second, its frequency last.

whyWrong.A: No other language is compared with Ojibwe, and no question is raised or answered.
whyWrong.B: The text never claims these are the most frequent words, never discusses translation difficulty, and never mentions other target languages.
whyWrong.D: Reduplication is defined but never described as controversial, and no scholarly dispute is resolved.

tips: For structure questions, match each stage of the choice to a specific sentence; if a stage has no sentence behind it, the choice is out.

whyCorrect: The line in question sets the speaker against the whole landscape: the fields are asleep and his heart alone wakes. That word does the work, marking him as the only waking thing in the scene while evening comes on. So the line establishes his solitude as he takes in the evening, which is the mood the rest of the poem, with night wandering and the moon in her hand, builds on.

whyWrong.B: The poem states no preference between the fields and the harbour; both simply appear in the scene.
whyWrong.C: Nothing in the poem mentions other people or any attitude of theirs toward the countryside.
whyWrong.D: The poem gives no cause for the speaker's wakefulness, and the waking heart is a figure for alertness rather than a report of getting out of bed.

commonMistakes: Reading alone as modifying only the heart's activity rather than marking the speaker as the sole waking presence in the landscape.

whyCorrect: The text defines a loanword in its first sentence and then spends the rest of its length tracing two of them. Tomato runs from Nahuatl through Spanish into English; maize runs from Taíno through Spanish into English. The shared shape of those two histories, not any detail within either, is the point.

whyWrong.A: The direction is reversed: the words moved from Indigenous languages into Spanish and then into English, never through English first.
whyWrong.B: The text gives one word from each language and makes no claim about how many words Spanish borrowed from either.
whyWrong.C: Both words kept their meanings, the plant and the corn plant; no change in meaning is described.

tips: A main-idea answer should cover the whole text; here that means both words, not one.

whyCorrect: The text says Barragan's career moved through distinct phases, then supplies the pivot: after traveling to the United States and Europe and absorbing international architectural debate, he began working with functionalism and modernism. The two buildings are there to show the change, with the unadorned geometry of the church set against the historically inspired earlier houses. The main idea is that shift and what caused it.

whyWrong.A: Only the church is described as functionalist and modernist; the earlier houses are the historically inspired contrast, and the text calls neither a paragon.
whyWrong.B: It reverses the comparison, since the earlier houses are the conventional ones and the church is the new departure.
whyWrong.C: The modernist turn comes after his travels, not at the start, and the text never says he abandoned it.

commonMistakes: Choosing a statement about one of the two buildings; both are evidence for a claim about the career as a whole.

whyCorrect: The hinge is the sentence saying Tagaq is not the only Indigenous writer doing this. That turns the passage from a profile of one writer into a claim about a pattern, and Stephen Graham Jones blending Blackfeet oral tradition with horror is the second case supporting it. The main idea has to be that pattern: recent Indigenous writers combining traditional stories with popular genres.

whyWrong.A: The text says nothing about non-Indigenous authors or what they should do.
whyWrong.B: Sales are never mentioned; the praise described comes from critics and fellow writers.
whyWrong.D: No influence of Tagaq on other writers is claimed, and Jones is Indigenous, not the non-Indigenous author this describes.

tips: When a passage says a subject is not the only one, the main idea is almost always the general pattern rather than the first example.

whyCorrect: You need a line that shows the banker in visible distress. D gives it directly: he lies down but his tears and emotion keep him awake for hours. Distress is stated in the quotation itself, which is what illustrating the claim requires.

whyWrong.A: Breaking seals and turning a key describes an action, and cautious is not upset.
whyWrong.B: It sets the hour and the quiet of the house; the banker only listens, showing no emotion.
whyWrong.C: It shows him delighted, the opposite of upset.

commonMistakes: Picking a tense or atmospheric line because it feels dramatic; the quotation has to show the specific state the claim names.

whyCorrect: The student's claim is that time is universally mapped onto space relative to the speaker's own body, the way English uses front and back. To weaken it you need a group mapping time onto something outside the body. B does exactly that: Yupno speakers point downhill for the past no matter which way they are facing, so their reference is the terrain, not their own orientation.

whyWrong.A: Shared grammatical structures say nothing about whether the spatial reference is tied to the speaker's body.
whyWrong.C: Opposite directions for past and future is what an egocentric front/back axis would produce, so it supports the claim rather than weakening it.
whyWrong.D: How often speakers gesture is a matter of frequency; the claim is about what the gestures are anchored to.

tips: The phrase regardless of which way they are facing is the giveaway that a reference frame is not egocentric.

whyCorrect: The second team says the sounds are made mainly to communicate with other caterpillars of the same species. Communication needs a listener, so the fastest way to challenge the claim is to show there was no one to hear. C does that twice over: the sound-producing species normally live alone, and in the experiment they were tested in isolation, so the clicks and whistles cannot have been aimed at a conspecific.

whyWrong.A: Sound appearing only once an attack begins shows the trigger, but a warning call to relatives would also be triggered by an attack, so it does not rule out communication.
whyWrong.B: It describes the species that stayed silent under attack, so it says nothing about why the sound-producing species make noise.
whyWrong.D: Sounds inaudible to bats, lizards, and birds undercut the predator-defense explanation, which pushes toward the second team's claim rather than against it.

tips: To challenge a claim about a signal's audience, look for evidence that the audience was absent.

whyCorrect: Set the old belief against the new count. Researchers had thought defensive ultrasound was confined to tiger moths, hawkmoths, and a single geometer species, and Barber's team found it in 52 genera drawn from most families of large-bodied moths, several of them geometers. That is the same defense turning up in far more of the group than anyone had recorded, so the conclusion is about how widespread the strategy is.

whyWrong.A: The study tested only whether moths clicked in response to bat echolocation; genera that did not click may still have other anti-bat defenses, and 52 of 252 supports breadth rather than absence.
whyWrong.B: Every click discussed here is a response to played-back bat echolocation, so the data point to predator defense, not to some other purpose.
whyWrong.C: No other evasion strategy is described anywhere in the text, so nothing supports calling ultrasound one option among a range.

commonMistakes: Reading 52 of 252 as a small fraction and inferring most moths lack the defense; the finding is measured against the previous belief of three groups, not against the whole.

whyCorrect: The argument has a gap in it and the last sentence asks you to close it. Songs carry ecological knowledge, and some expressions exist only in songs, yet preservation efforts have concentrated on spoken language. If the goal is a comprehensive record, the missing step is to bring songs into the preservation work itself.

whyWrong.A: The text never ranks ecological knowledge against other kinds of information, so this comparison is unsupported.
whyWrong.B: It contradicts the passage, which says some expressions appear only in songs rather than being drawn from speech.
whyWrong.D: Comparing the music of the Warlpiri and the Sakha is a research question, not a way to secure the information at risk.

tips: When the text ends with therefore ... they must, the answer is the action that repairs the shortfall the passage just identified.

whyCorrect: There are two complete statements here: Coalition is the term for a group of male lions, and across the Greater Kruger National Park of South Africa, many coalitions vie for territory. The second one is independent even though it opens with a prepositional phrase, so joining the two takes a comma plus a coordinating conjunction.

whyWrong.A: With nothing at the blank, the prepositional phrase attaches to lions and the rest of the sentence becomes a comma splice.
whyWrong.B: A comma alone cannot join two independent clauses.
whyWrong.C: and without the comma leaves the two independent clauses fused; the comma later in the sentence belongs to the introductory phrase, not to the join.

commonMistakes: Mistaking the comma after South Africa for the one that joins the clauses; it only closes the introductory phrase.

whyCorrect: Two things are happening at the blank. The list race, gender, history, and memory has to finish, and then a second independent clause, she is credited with expanding the horizons of conceptual photographic art, has to be joined on. C closes the list with memory and then joins the clauses with a comma plus and.

whyWrong.A: memory and runs the list straight into the next clause with no punctuation, fusing two independent clauses.
whyWrong.B: A comma alone between the two independent clauses is a splice.
whyWrong.D: With no punctuation at all the second clause runs on from the first.

tips: When a sentence already contains a list, check separately whether what follows the list is a new independent clause; it usually is when a new subject appears.

whyCorrect: The clause before the blank makes a general claim, that many writers of other forms are still well known, and the clause after it supplies the case that proves it: Koulsy Lamko, a celebrated playwright from Chad. A colon is the mark for introducing an explanation or example after a complete statement, and both sides here are complete.

whyWrong.A: With no punctuation, two independent clauses run together.
whyWrong.C: and without a comma fuses the clauses, and it also loses the example relationship the colon expresses.
whyWrong.D: A comma alone between two independent clauses is a splice.

tips: A colon needs a complete sentence on its left; check that before deciding it is too strong a mark.

whyCorrect: Read past the blank to find the sentence's real verb: Most of the original two- or three-digit codes ... later changed in response to geopolitical circumstances. Changed is the main verb, so the blank cannot hold another conjugated verb. It needs the past participle assigned, forming a reduced modifier meaning the codes that were assigned by the committee.

whyWrong.A: were assigned is finite, leaving the subject with two main verbs and no conjunction.
whyWrong.B: had been assigned is finite for the same reason.
whyWrong.D: would be assigned is finite and also puts the assignment in the future relative to a past that the sentence never establishes.

commonMistakes: Stopping at by the committee and never reaching later changed, which is what makes the finite options impossible.

whyCorrect: The end of the sentence gives it away: after the long list of contents there is a new subject and verb, this magazine publicized the work of influential avant-garde writers. That is a full independent clause, so the first statement, Among the small magazines ... was the Poetry Review of America, has to be closed off with a period. The capitalized participle Edited then opens the modifier that leads into the new subject.

whyWrong.B: A colon after a complete statement is possible, but what follows still ends in an independent clause, so the modifier and this magazine publicized collide.
whyWrong.C: The comma turns the rest into a modifier hanging off the first clause, leaving this magazine publicized spliced on.
whyWrong.D: With no punctuation the participial phrase attaches directly to the magazine's name and the final clause is still run on.

tips: When the sentence ends with a fresh subject like this magazine, everything before it must already be a finished sentence plus a modifier.

whyCorrect: Two things fix the tense. The sentence opens with During the 20th century, a period that is over, and the main verb is already past: the three states each selected a dinosaur. The blank names that same act again for Montana, so it has to be the simple past chose.

whyWrong.A: is choosing is present progressive, putting a completed 20th-century decision in progress now.
whyWrong.B: will choose places the choice in the future, contradicting during the 20th century.
whyWrong.C: chooses is simple present and clashes with selected earlier in the same sentence.

tips: A dated time marker plus an existing past-tense verb in the sentence decides these questions before you weigh anything else.

whyCorrect: The engineers advised against multiple track widths, and the next sentence says regional officials could not settle on one width, which is exactly what the engineers warned against. The advice was given and then not followed, so the transition has to mark that the outcome went against the warning.

whyWrong.A: In other words would make the second sentence a restatement of the warning, but it reports what officials did, not what engineers said.
whyWrong.B: Similarly claims the two sentences run in the same direction, when the second undercuts the first.
whyWrong.C: For this reason makes the disagreement a consequence of the warning, reversing the logic; the disagreement happened in spite of it. Note that Thus already opens the following sentence, which is where the real consequence appears.

commonMistakes: Assuming a warning is always followed by its consequence; here the middle sentence reports the warning being ignored.

whyCorrect: Compare the two sentences word for word. The first says that whatever the topic, Montaigne challenges his own ideas, beliefs, and values; the second says that regardless of subject matter, he questions his own perspective. That is the same claim restated with added emphasis, which is what Indeed signals.

whyWrong.A: For example requires a specific instance, but the second sentence is just as general as the first and names no essay.
whyWrong.B: At that time points to a particular moment, and no moment has been established.
whyWrong.D: However demands a contrast, and the two sentences agree completely.

tips: If you can swap the two sentences without changing the meaning, you are dealing with restatement or emphasis, not example or contrast.

whyCorrect: The clause before the semicolon says the plant pulls a large amount of cadmium out of the soil and locks it away in its roots and shoots. The clause after states the soil's cadmium concentration falling. The second follows from the first as its direct result, so the transition needs to mark consequence.

whyWrong.A: specifically would make the second clause a narrower detail of the first, but it reports a separate outcome in the soil rather than a finer point about the plant.
whyWrong.B: nevertheless signals contrast, and falling soil cadmium is exactly what absorption would predict.
whyWrong.C: in addition treats the two as independent facts, missing that one causes the other.

tips: Ask whether the second clause would still be true if the first were not; if it depends on the first, you need a consequence word.

whyCorrect: The goal has two constraints: introduce Walker so a discussion of his career can follow, and address readers who already know the MBC project. That means the sentence should place Walker within the project and stop, without spending words explaining what the project is for. C does that and leaves the career discussion still to come.

whyWrong.A: It turns attention to the many other composers in the directory, which leads away from Walker rather than into his career.
whyWrong.B: It gives only his birth and death years and attributes them oddly to the project, which sets up an obituary rather than a career discussion.
whyWrong.D: It explains the project's aim of inspiring future composers, information an audience already familiar with MBC does not need.

tips: When the goal names an audience that already knows something, drop the choice that explains that thing.

whyCorrect: To emphasize a difference the sentence must name both people and put one detail of each in opposition. B does it on instrument: Insel played viola, Quiñones played guitar, joined by whereas. The shared context is acknowledged briefly and then the contrast carries the sentence.

whyWrong.A: It gives release dates, and the comparison is between two albums rather than between the two musicians.
whyWrong.C: It describes the albums and never mentions either musician.
whyWrong.D: It states what the two have in common, which is a similarity.

commonMistakes: Choosing a sentence that mentions both names; the goal needs a feature of one set against the matching feature of the other.

whyCorrect: The goal asks how DLS cures objects, so the sentence has to get the mechanism right and in order: UV light images projected into a pool of liquid resin, curing the object one layer at a time, and then a final bake in an oven to finish the curing. C is the only choice that keeps all three stages and assigns each to the right agent.

whyWrong.A: It says the machine cures objects by passing through a dead zone, but the dead zone is a gap that lets resin and oxygen flow; it is not what does the curing.
whyWrong.B: It has the resin solidifying and then passing through the dead zone, reversing the arrangement, and it puts the completion of curing in the dead zone rather than in the oven.
whyWrong.D: It describes the UV light itself as solidifying layer by layer and then being baked, which misassigns the action to the light instead of to the resin object.

tips: For a how-it-works goal, check that each step has the right subject; a choice can name every stage and still describe the wrong thing doing them.

whyCorrect: Read what happens on either side of the word. Tom arrives with whitewash and a brush, and immediately after he surveys the fence his gladness drains away, with the next line giving the dimensions that dismayed him: thirty yards long and nine feet high. He is taking in the size of the job, so surveyed means looked over or examined.

whyWrong.A: Complimented would mean praising the fence, which cannot produce the deep melancholy that follows.
whyWrong.C: Converted means changed into something else, and Tom has not touched the fence yet.
whyWrong.D: Organized means arranged, but a stretch of board fence is not something he puts in order by looking at it.

tips: For word-in-context items, use the sentence right after the word; here the fence's measurements show he was sizing up the task.

whyCorrect: The paragraph is about how the public came to see film. Filmmakers wanted the public to embrace the medium, and the last sentence says critics who compared film to drama could help legitimize it as an art form. Legitimizing changes how something is regarded, so what critics were being used to influence was the public's view of cinema.

whyWrong.A: Contribution to would mean the public was adding something to cinema, but the passage is about what the public thought of it.
whyWrong.C: Reproduction of means copying, which the public is not doing to the world of cinema.
whyWrong.D: Application to suggests the public putting something to use in cinema, which nothing in the passage describes.

tips: The last sentence often names the effect the blank must describe; legitimize points straight at opinion.

whyCorrect: The first sentence stretches from monumental sculpture at one end to street murals at the other, and the second says this art can satisfy any art lover. What makes it able to satisfy anyone is its range, so the blank has to name that range. Breadth of does.

whyWrong.B: Controversy over introduces a dispute the passage never mentions, and disputed art would not be what satisfies every viewer.
whyWrong.C: Confusion about is likewise negative and unsupported.
whyWrong.D: Apathy toward contradicts the sentence, since indifference cannot satisfy an art lover.

commonMistakes: Overlooking that thus ties the blank to the from-sculpture-to-street-art span in the previous sentence.

whyCorrect: The subject of the sentence is a pair of obstacles: nocturnal visits are hard to document and attention has gone to daytime pollinators instead. Obstacles like those produce a shortage of information, and the closing clause confirms it, since Anderson's team had to use infrared technology to fill the gap. A dearth means a scarcity.

whyWrong.A: An abatement is a reduction of something already in progress, but the point is that this information was never gathered.
whyWrong.B: An aggregation is a gathering together, the opposite of what these difficulties would cause.
whyWrong.D: A dissonance is a clash between things, and no conflicting findings are described.

tips: When a sentence names obstacles to collecting evidence, the blank almost always names a lack of it.

whyCorrect: The second sentence spells out why Derrane received the fellowship: he has contributed so much to the arts. Since the fellowship honors artists for whatever fills the blank, the blank must name that kind of contribution. Achievements is the only choice describing what an artist has accomplished.

whyWrong.B: Suspicions are doubts, which no award honors.
whyWrong.C: Assumptions are unproven beliefs, unrelated to artistic contribution.
whyWrong.D: Predictions concern the future, while the fellowship recognizes work already done.

tips: When a second sentence gives the reason for an award, the blank restates that reason in a single noun.

whyCorrect: Everything in the text serves one job: a thermopolium was recently found at Pompeii, it contains food remains, artworks, and decorations, those items illuminate daily life, and one of them is a jar that probably held a meat and seafood stew. That is the reporting of a new archaeological find and what it shows.

whyWrong.A: No political system, ancient or modern, is mentioned.
whyWrong.C: The text describes a shop and its contents, not weather or climate.
whyWrong.D: Artworks are listed among the finds, but nothing modern appears for them to be compared with.

tips: When every sentence adds detail to a single find, the purpose is to present it, not to argue anything about it.

whyCorrect: The first two sentences set up a study and its numbers: 53.5 percent park use in Panama City against 44.7 percent in Caracas. The last sentence takes up one candidate explanation for that gap, better access to desired nonpark amenities near parks in Panama City, and rules it out, because Panama City respondents actually reported much lower access. So the structure is study, then a proposed explanation, then its rejection.

whyWrong.A: Survey methodology is never discussed, and the finding is not attributed to how the data were collected.
whyWrong.B: No open question about park planning is posed, and the text ends by eliminating an explanation rather than answering a question.
whyWrong.D: Both cities come from the same study, and the Caracas numbers are used for contrast, not to corroborate anything.

commonMistakes: Reading the last sentence as offering the explanation when the phrase can't be explained by is doing the opposite.

whyCorrect: Put the two texts together as premises. Text 1 supplies the facts: the northern pike faces significantly worse outcomes under predicted warming, while the white-tailed deer should withstand it and likely will not need the conservation efforts the pike will. Text 2 supplies the principle: agencies cannot address every threat and must direct effort toward the species most in need. Applying the principle to the facts gives priority to the pike over the deer.

whyWrong.A: Neither text discusses influencing temperatures; both are about managing species under warming that is assumed.
whyWrong.C: Text 1 comes from a tribal conservation group and Text 2 from government agencies, but neither text argues that combining their resources improves outcomes.
whyWrong.D: Text 1 says the deer likely will not require such efforts, and Text 2 says agencies must choose, so committing to programs for both contradicts them.

tips: For both-authors-agree questions, look for the statement that needs one fact from each text; a claim resting on only one text is usually wrong.

whyCorrect: Note exactly what the author concedes and what the author denies. The concession is explicit: income of course constrained fuel choice. The denial is that income is the whole story, since Ouedraogo found other factors, such as how often certain dishes are cooked, also shaping decisions. Calling the energy ladder reductive means it is incomplete, not false, so income accounts for part but not all of the variation.

whyWrong.A: The text is about which fuels households pick, not how much they use, and it says income does constrain that choice.
whyWrong.B: The author disputes how much the model explains, not the reason income matters; no alternative mechanism for income's effect is proposed.
whyWrong.D: The concession income of course constrained fuel choice directly contradicts the claim that it does not.

commonMistakes: Treating a criticism of a model as a rejection of its central variable; reductive means oversimplified, not wrong.

whyCorrect: The question asks only what the text says she led, so find the sentence with a leadership word in it. The last sentence states that she was the leader of what became known as the Cambridge movement. The cochair role at the Cambridge Nonviolent Action Committee is a related detail, but the movement is what the text names her as leading.

whyWrong.A: No business appears anywhere in the text; her work described is political organizing.
whyWrong.C: The protests described concern racial equality, not environmental protection.
whyWrong.D: Donna is described as joining protests; nothing is said about her school or her mother running it.

tips: For an according to the text question, locate the exact sentence rather than reasoning from the general topic.

whyCorrect: The claim needs a quotation that puts the narrator's outlook beside Avey's and shows them differing. D does both in one sentence: Avey's indifference to things is set directly against the narrator's statement that he was ambitious. Only that pairing gives you the contrast the claim describes.

whyWrong.A: It describes dawn over Washington and mentions neither character's attitude toward life.
whyWrong.B: Avey's silence is described, but the narrator offers no attitude of his own to contrast with it.
whyWrong.C: It reports a moment of physical closeness rather than any difference in outlook.

commonMistakes: Choosing a quotation that characterizes Avey alone; a contrast claim requires both sides to appear.

whyCorrect: The conclusion links two things: how much language a dog has been exposed to, and how well it tells a familiar language from an unfamiliar one. So the supporting finding must measure the familiar-versus-unfamiliar gap and show it varying with exposure. D does exactly that, with the gap between responses to the accustomed and unaccustomed languages largest in older dogs, who have had the most exposure.

whyWrong.A: It compares the familiar language with the scrambled recording, which tests speech against non-speech rather than one language against another.
whyWrong.B: It shows dogs of every age distinguishing the two languages equally well, which leaves exposure with nothing to explain.
whyWrong.C: It compares the unfamiliar language with the scrambled recording, so the familiar language never enters the comparison the conclusion is about.

tips: Match the finding to the exact comparison in the conclusion; here the scrambled recording is a control, not one of the two things being distinguished.

whyCorrect: Translate the hypothesis into predictions about these two birds. M. barbatus forages in dense vegetation, so its field of vision is poor and an inverse relationship predicts high sensitivity to other species' alarm calls. P. saturatus forages in the open with a wide field of view, so it should be relatively insensitive. D reports precisely that split: the antshrike's alarm call moves M. barbatus and leaves P. saturatus unmoved.

whyWrong.A: Neither species reacts, so there is no difference in sensitivity for field of vision to explain.
whyWrong.B: It compares M. barbatus with other species that forage the same way, which holds field of vision constant instead of varying it.
whyWrong.C: It compares two different alarm calls heard by one species, so it says nothing about how sensitivity varies with field of vision.

tips: For a hypothesis about an inverse relationship, you need two subjects that differ on the first variable and differ oppositely on the second.

whyCorrect: The final clause reports what Lepofsky and colleagues actually established: the clam-garden practice described in the songs tracked with rising clam yield and abundance even under heavier harvesting. That means the songs carry a technique that worked for cultivating a food staple. So the demonstrated point is that Indigenous songs preserve effective methods for producing sustenance.

whyWrong.A: Calling this the defining characteristic of a people's music is far broader than a single finding about clam gardens can show.
whyWrong.B: It reverses the reasoning into a claim about why the songs were composed, which the evidence about yields does not address.
whyWrong.C: Clam species are never distinguished; the study concerns yield and abundance, not taxonomy.

commonMistakes: Choosing the option that speculates about the songs' motives rather than the one stating what the archaeological and song evidence jointly show.

whyCorrect: The last sentence introduces one specific difference between the two studies' subjects: captive animals spend far more time around humans than wild animals do. Since the captive study found right-handedness and the wild study did not, and humans are overwhelmingly right-handed, the conclusion the passage is steering toward is that human contact may have helped produce the captive animals' right-hand bias.

whyWrong.A: Differing standards for measuring handedness would be a different explanation entirely, and the sentence sets up human contact, not methodology.
whyWrong.C: Sample size is never mentioned, and the passage gives no numbers of individuals in either study.
whyWrong.D: Same problem: nothing in the text bears on how many wild chimpanzees were observed.

tips: The word therefore means the completion must follow from the fact stated immediately before it, not from anything else in the passage.

whyCorrect: Strip out the interrupting phrase and the subject is clear: more writers from Guinea ... have begun to reach audiences. Writers is plural, so the verb must be plural, and in recent years calls for the present perfect, describing something that started earlier and continues now.

whyWrong.A: is beginning is singular, agreeing with Diallo inside the interrupter rather than with the real subject.
whyWrong.B: has begun has the right tense but is singular.
whyWrong.D: begins is singular and its simple present does not fit in recent years.

commonMistakes: Letting the phrase including Diallo set the verb's number; a phrase between commas never contains the subject.

whyCorrect: The description of Martinez as the first woman in the role is an interrupting element, and the sentence already closes it with a dash before took office. Punctuation around an interrupter has to match at both ends, so the opening mark must be a dash too.

whyWrong.A: A comma at the start and a dash at the end are mismatched marks around the same interrupter.
whyWrong.B: A colon cannot pair with a closing dash, and it would also break the subject away from its verb.
whyWrong.C: With nothing at the start, the closing dash has no partner and the interrupter is only half enclosed.

tips: Look at the punctuation the sentence already provides at the far end of the interrupter; it dictates what the blank needs.

whyCorrect: Both halves here are complete sentences. Before the blank: Butterfly ... attempts to make use of the entire visual light spectrum. After it: sporting rainbow-striped goggles, the rainbow-hued swimmer splashes through a wavy rainbow of water, which has its own subject and verb behind an introductory participial phrase. The second half spells out how the painting uses the whole spectrum, so a colon, which needs a complete statement on its left and introduces an elaboration, is the right mark.

whyWrong.A: while attaches the goggles phrase to the painting's attempt, and the final clause about the swimmer is then left running on.
whyWrong.B: The comma plus while has the same problem and leaves the rainbow-hued swimmer splashes spliced onto the sentence.
whyWrong.D: With no punctuation the two independent clauses fuse.

tips: A colon is available whenever the words to its left form a complete sentence and the words to its right explain them.

whyCorrect: Find the main verb first: it is led, in led developers to invent the dual-core chip. That verb needs a subject, and the blank has to create one. The gerund phrase Hitting a power wall in which more heat was produced than could be efficiently dissipated is a noun phrase and serves as that subject, so the sentence reads as an event leading to an invention.

whyWrong.B: When they hit makes a subordinate clause, after which led has no subject at all.
whyWrong.C: They hit supplies a second finite verb, so the sentence has hit and led with nothing joining them.
whyWrong.D: Upon hitting is a prepositional phrase, which cannot serve as a subject, leaving led stranded.

commonMistakes: Assuming the noun right before the verb is the subject; here a power wall sits inside the phrase that is the subject.

whyCorrect: The word that after It is widely known opens a clause, and a clause needs a subject and a conjugated verb. The subject is MoMA, singular, so the verb is the singular present houses.

whyWrong.A: housing is a participle, leaving the that clause with no verb.
whyWrong.B: to house is an infinitive, which also cannot serve as the clause's verb after that.
whyWrong.C: to have housed is an infinitive as well, and its perfect form would wrongly place the collection in the past.

tips: After known that, expect a full clause; only a conjugated verb can complete one.

whyCorrect: Everything after the blank is a complete sentence in its own right: the word lasso comes from lazo, and cinch comes from cincho. Everything before it is complete too, ending at come from Spanish. So the blank has to end one sentence and start the next, which only the period does.

whyWrong.B: The opening parenthesis is never closed, and a parenthetical cannot swallow the rest of the sentence.
whyWrong.C: With no punctuation the two independent clauses run together.
whyWrong.D: A question mark makes a statement into a question, and nothing here is being asked.

commonMistakes: Being distracted by the parentheses already in the sentence around the glosses (a rope) and (a belt); those are separate and already closed.

whyCorrect: The first sentence denies something, that kho kho was a medal sport in 1936, and the second supplies what was true instead, that it appeared as a demonstration sport. A negative followed by the correct alternative calls for Rather.

whyWrong.A: For example would make the second sentence an instance of the first, but the first states what did not happen.
whyWrong.C: Thus marks a consequence, and appearing as a demonstration sport does not follow from not being a medal sport.
whyWrong.D: Additionally would add a separate fact, missing that the second sentence corrects the first.

tips: When one sentence says not X and the next says Y, the transition is a correction word.

whyCorrect: The first sentence stresses how primitive the 1920 method was, just a cardboard cutout and a piece of string. The second reports that it came within a few miles of a modern computer calculation. Crude tools producing an accurate result is a reversal of what the setup leads you to expect, so the transition marks concession.

whyWrong.B: Similarly claims the second sentence runs parallel to the first, but accuracy is the surprise, not a repetition.
whyWrong.C: In other words would make the second sentence a restatement, and it introduces new information about the comparison with the computer result.
whyWrong.D: Fittingly says the outcome suits what came before, which reverses the surprise the sentence is built on; the phrase apparently crude is the signal.

commonMistakes: Reading apparently crude as an insult to the method rather than as the setup for a contrast.

whyCorrect: The first sentence names an assumption, that the offshore farm makes the same energy as comparable land farms. The second corrects it: because wind is faster over open water, Amrumbank West's turbines produce more. A stated assumption followed by the truth requires a correction word, and Actually is the one.

whyWrong.B: For example would need the second sentence to illustrate the assumption, but it overturns it.
whyWrong.C: Therefore would make the higher output follow from the assumption of equal output, which is a contradiction.
whyWrong.D: Finally marks the end of a sequence, and no sequence has been laid out.

tips: The phrase one might assume nearly always signals that the next sentence corrects the assumption.

whyCorrect: The goal is a difference between the two musicians, so the sentence must name both and oppose one detail of each. B does it on instrument, guitar for Quiñones and cello for Catchings, with whereas making the contrast the point of the sentence.

whyWrong.A: It states what the two have in common, which is a similarity rather than a difference.
whyWrong.C: It covers only Quiñones and then compares release dates of two albums.
whyWrong.D: It describes the albums and never mentions either musician.

commonMistakes: Accepting any sentence that names both musicians; the goal requires their differing contributions set against each other.

whyCorrect: The notes give two shared traits, that both works are LED light sculptures and that both are by Amoros, and two differing ones, material style and size. Since the goal is similarity, the sentence has to be built from the shared traits. A puts both sculptures under the same artist and the same medium and adds nothing that divides them.

whyWrong.B: It sets the smooth domes against the tangled tubes, which is an explicit contrast.
whyWrong.C: It describes Uros House only, so there is no second work to be similar to.
whyWrong.D: It compares the two sizes to show one is far larger, another contrast.

commonMistakes: Reading the goal too quickly and reaching for the choice with the most vivid comparison; the vivid ones here are all differences.

whyCorrect: The goal asks for an example of a particle physicist whose work centers on neutrinos, so the sentence has to name a person, identify him as a particle physicist, and tie his research to neutrinos. C does all three: Francis Halzen, particle physicist, known for discovering high-energy astrophysical neutrinos.

whyWrong.A: It describes the research without naming anyone, so no physicist is exemplified.
whyWrong.B: It refers to particle physicists in general; the example it offers is a topic of study, not a person.
whyWrong.D: It defines neutrinos and never mentions a researcher.

tips: When the goal says an example of a person, only a choice naming an individual can work.

whyCorrect: The sentence turns on but: Marquis accomplished a great deal, yet her standing in historical memory compares unfavorably with someone else's. The comparison point is Machado, whose achievement ends with a deed for which she will always be remembered. Against a memory that is permanent, Marquis's has to be shakier, so uncertain is the fit.

whyWrong.A: Enduring would make her memory more lasting than one described as permanent, contradicting the contrast.
whyWrong.C: Conspicuous means highly visible, again crediting her with the stronger place in memory.
whyWrong.D: Deserving shifts to merit, but the passage already grants she accomplished much; what is at stake is whether she is remembered.

commonMistakes: Anchoring on undoubtedly accomplished much and missing that but turns the sentence toward a shortfall.

whyCorrect: The sentence opens by calling these entries hoaxes played as jokes by mischievous users, so when the site finally recognized them for what they were and deleted them, what it recognized was that they were jokes. Pranks is the word that matches hoaxes perpetrated as jokes.

whyWrong.A: An enhancement is an improvement, and an improvement would not be deleted.
whyWrong.B: Revelations are disclosures of truth, the opposite of fabricated entries.
whyWrong.D: Analyses are studies of something, which fictitious biography entries are not.

tips: The blank restates a word already in the sentence; scan back for hoaxes and jokes before weighing the choices.

whyCorrect: Work out which item causes which. The stated fact is that features enabling flight limit top speed less than features suited to running do; the speed gap between the antelope and the falcon is what that fact produces. The blank names what the difference is with respect to that fact, so it has to be the effect, a consequence of it.

whyWrong.B: An objective makes the difference a goal, but neither animal is aiming at anything.
whyWrong.C: A repudiation would have the difference rejecting the fact, when the fact accounts for it.
whyWrong.D: An explanation reverses the direction: the fact explains the difference, not the reverse.

commonMistakes: Choosing an explanation because the sentence is explanatory; check which of the two items is doing the explaining.

whyCorrect: The second sentence gives you the alternative to the blank: if instead the bear died out before humans arrived, some other cause was at work. The blank must therefore describe the opposite case, the extinction and the human arrival falling at the same time. Coincided with says exactly that, and radiocarbon dating is a tool for comparing dates.

whyWrong.A: Compensated for means made up for a loss, which an extinction cannot do for an arrival.
whyWrong.C: Developed into would mean the extinction turned into the arrival of humans, which is incoherent.
whyWrong.D: Clashed with suggests conflict between the two, but dating establishes timing, not confrontation.

tips: When the next sentence starts with if instead, it names the alternative; the blank has to be its opposite.

whyCorrect: The example at the end tells you what the blank names: a well-executed marketing campaign that pushed a Danielle Steel novel to fourth-best-selling of 1994. The blank has to be the general category that campaign belongs to, and marketing is a form of publicity.
