whyWrong.A: Originality is a quality of the writing, not something a marketing campaign supplies.
whyWrong.C: Complexity also describes the book itself and has no link to the campaign.
whyWrong.D: Practicality describes usefulness, which neither the sentence nor the example raises.

tips: When a sentence gives a specific example, the blank is usually the general term that example falls under.

whyCorrect: The passage is built as a two-part comparison. The sermon is spoken, meant for the moment, and lasts only as long as memory holds it; the printed book is a permanent record anyone can own, consult, cite, and pass on long after its author is dead. Everything in the text serves that side-by-side contrast of two ways of communicating.

whyWrong.A: It is about forms of communication, not about which artists critics keep discussing.
whyWrong.B: No groups of scholars appear, and no contribution to society is assessed.
whyWrong.C: The passage compares what each form can do, never how often either is used.

tips: When a passage sets one thing against another with a semicolon, the purpose is nearly always to lay out the differences.

whyCorrect: The narrator says there is a chance she will make the freshman team, then spends the rest of the passage justifying that chance: she is small but quick, wiry, and tough, and she can dodge under other players' feet to grab the ball while they are jumping. Those details are her reasons, so the purpose is to explain why she thinks she has a shot.

whyWrong.A: No other sport is mentioned.
whyWrong.B: Her dodging is offered as evidence about her, not as instruction in how the game is played.
whyWrong.C: The passage says the team is being organized but never describes a selection process.

commonMistakes: Treating the description of her playing style as the point; it is the support for the claim in the first sentence.

whyCorrect: Text 2 gives a specific diagnosis for the old view: ornithologists worked mostly near universities in the temperate northern hemisphere, and female song is less common there than in the tropics. So the assumption in Text 1 came from where the observations were made. Odom and colleagues would say the belief was shaped by researchers' choice of study locations.

whyWrong.A: Text 2 blames the geography of the research, not a preference for observing male birds; the bias it names is in the sites, not in the sex of the subjects.
whyWrong.B: The evolutionary purposes of male song are never disputed in Text 2, which is about how widespread female song is.
whyWrong.C: No claim is made that male song serves different purposes in temperate zones than in the tropics; the regional difference concerns female song.

commonMistakes: Picking the answer that sounds like generic research bias instead of the specific bias Text 2 identifies.

whyCorrect: Reductive means it boils something complicated down to too little. The energy ladder pins fuel choice mainly on one household characteristic, income. Heltberg's Guatemala study found fuel use to be varied and flexible and shaped by several influences, including local prices of different sources. The criticism, then, is that one variable is standing in for many.

whyWrong.A: Heltberg did not find that households ignore income; the text says only that other factors also matter.
whyWrong.B: Nothing in the study is described as showing fuel types used in equal proportion, and displacement is not what the author objects to.
whyWrong.C: The text never compares which factors operate in Guatemala against which operate in Costa Rica; Costa Rica supplies the opening statistic only.

tips: When an author calls a model reductive, look for the contrast between one cause in the model and many causes in the evidence.

whyCorrect: The question wants both halves: the finding and its explanation. The finding is that bright moonlight inhibits the bats' activity, so they do less on bright nights. The explanation is a cost-benefit trade: the extra light does not raise foraging success enough to be worth the greater chance of being spotted by owls or hawks. B states both accurately.

whyWrong.A: It reverses the finding, having the bats more active in bright light, and denies the higher detection risk the text names.
whyWrong.C: It uses the wrong comparison; the bats' risk is weighed against their own foraging gains, not against how visible lemurs are.
whyWrong.D: It describes the lemurs, who are a contrasting aside, and misstates their case as one of greater risk rather than a different balance of reward and risk.

tips: When a question asks for a finding and a reason, check both halves of the choice; a correct finding with a wrong reason is still wrong.

whyCorrect: The student claims that everyone maps time onto space relative to their own body, as Spanish speakers do with left and right. To weaken that you need a group anchoring time to something outside themselves. D provides it: Yupno speakers point uphill for the future no matter which way they face, so the reference is the landscape, not the speaker.

whyWrong.A: Opposite directions for past and future is what an egocentric axis would produce, so it supports the claim.
whyWrong.B: Shared grammar says nothing about whether the spatial frame is body-based.
whyWrong.C: How many gestures speakers make is a matter of quantity, not of what the gestures are anchored to.

tips: Regardless of which way they are facing is the phrase that rules out a body-centered reference frame.

whyCorrect: Ambivalence needs both attitudes at once, in the same lines. D has them: the speaker reads poetry with a perfect contempt for it, which is the displeasure, and yet discovers that there is a place in it for the genuine, which is the merit. No other option holds both feelings together.

whyWrong.A: It argues that business documents and school-books should count as important, which is an inclusive claim rather than a mixed feeling about poetry.
whyWrong.B: It criticizes what half poets produce, so the displeasure is aimed at bad imitators, and no merit is granted alongside it.
whyWrong.C: It complains about derivative, unintelligible poems, again criticism without any answering appreciation.

commonMistakes: Choosing a quotation with a negative tone alone; the claim requires the negative and the positive in the same passage.

whyCorrect: The hypothesis is that measuring silver nanoparticles in the worm could stand in for measuring them in a vertebrate such as Atlantic salmon. A proxy only works if the substitute's readings track the original's. A supplies that: at similar exposure the two species accumulate similar amounts once body size is accounted for, so the worm's burden predicts the salmon's.

whyWrong.B: If worm levels track the environment while salmon levels stay flat, the two come apart, which destroys the substitution.
whyWrong.C: Tolerating higher concentrations without harm is about the worm's physiology, not about whether its readings mirror the salmon's.
whyWrong.D: It compares detecting a low concentration in one species with detecting a high one in the other, which does not establish that the two measurements correspond.

tips: To support a proxy claim, look for evidence that the stand-in and the original give matching measurements.

whyCorrect: The completion follows if this view is correct, so it must state what the ecosystem argument says the single-species approach gets wrong. That argument's core is that species are bound up with the climate, terrain, and other species around them. Concentrating only on M. guerreronis therefore leaves out how shifts in other Guerrero species affect its survival.

whyWrong.A: Better understanding of distribution would be a benefit, and the sentence is building toward a shortcoming.
whyWrong.B: Considering climatic effects on competing species is what the ecosystem approach adds, not something the single-species approach enables.
whyWrong.C: The single-species approach keeps the focus on M. guerreronis by definition, so it cannot shift attention away from it.

tips: Identify which approach the final sentence is about before choosing; the criticism must land on the single-species one.

whyCorrect: Trace the two products back to their alloys. Storage containers use the 300 series, which is a subtype of austenitic steel, and induction cookers use ferritic steel. The passage says austenitic steel, unlike ferritic, has a face-centered cubic crystalline structure produced by adding nickel. So container steel has that structure and cooker steel does not.

whyWrong.A: Magnetic properties come from the higher iron concentration in ferritic steel, which is the cooker alloy, so the container steel does not share them.
whyWrong.B: The 10.5 percent figure refers to chromium in ferritic steel, not manganese, and it is the 200 series used for indoor architecture that has more manganese, not the 300 series.
whyWrong.D: Nickel is what defines austenitic steel, so the 300 series container alloy has more nickel than the ferritic cooker alloy, not less.

commonMistakes: Carrying the 10.5 percent over to the wrong element; it is stated for chromium and only for ferritic steel.
